terms.definition: The Domain Name System: a distributed directory that translates names like example.com into IP addresses. Answers are cached at many levels.
The numeric address a machine uses on the internet, like 93.184.216.34 (IPv4) or a longer IPv6 address.
Transmission Control Protocol: delivers a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two machines, resending anything that gets lost.
User Datagram Protocol: sends individual packets with no delivery or ordering guarantees, which makes it simple and fast.
Transport Layer Security: encrypts a connection and proves the server’s identity. It is the “S” in HTTPS.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request–response protocol browsers and APIs use. A client sends a method and path; the server answers with a status code and a body.
A version of HTTP that sends many requests at once over a single connection (multiplexing) and compresses headers.
HTTP over QUIC, a transport built on UDP. A lost packet only delays its own stream instead of every request on the connection.
When one slow or lost item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it.
The time for a message to go from one machine to another and for the reply to come back.
Reusing an open connection for several requests, which avoids paying for a new TCP and TLS handshake each time.
Application Programming Interface: the contract one program offers others, listing the operations they can call and the data they exchange.
A style of HTTP API built around resources (nouns) identified by URLs and manipulated with standard methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.
A remote procedure call framework that sends compact binary messages (Protocol Buffers) over HTTP/2 and supports streaming.
A language-neutral way to define messages in a schema and encode them as compact binary.
A long-lived, two-way connection between browser and server, so either side can send messages at any time.
A one-way stream of messages from server to browser over a normal HTTP response.
The client makes a request that the server holds open until there is news, then the client immediately asks again.
Returning a large list in pages. Cursor-based pagination stays correct when items are added during browsing.
Changing an API without breaking existing clients, for example by adding fields instead of renaming them or by publishing /v2 alongside /v1.
A running program with its own memory space. Processes are isolated from each other by the operating system.
A unit of execution inside a process. Threads share the process’s memory, which makes them cheap to start but easy to get wrong.
When the CPU stops running one thread and starts another, saving and restoring their state. Frequent switching wastes time.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads, for example two threads both reading a counter as 5 and both writing 6.
A way to let only one thread at a time run a piece of code or touch a piece of data.
Two or more threads each waiting for a lock the other holds, so none of them can continue.
A single thread that waits for I/O events and runs a short handler for each. It serves many connections without a thread per connection.
Starting a read or write and doing other work until it finishes, instead of blocking a thread while waiting.
A fixed set of reusable threads that pick up tasks from a queue, which caps how much work runs at once.
A database that stores data in tables of rows and columns, links tables by keys and is queried with SQL.
An umbrella term for non-relational databases (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) that trade some features for scale or flexibility.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees a database transaction gives you.
A group of reads and writes that succeeds or fails as one unit.
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other’s unfinished work, from read committed to serializable.
An anomaly where two transactions each read the same data, make decisions based on it and write different rows, breaking a rule neither broke alone.
A database that stores values under keys and looks them up by key, which is simple and very fast.
A database that stores self-contained documents (often JSON) and can query fields inside them.
A database that groups data by row key into flexible column families, built for very large write-heavy workloads.
A database that stores nodes and the relationships between them and is fast at traversing those relationships.
Organizing tables so each fact is stored once, which avoids inconsistent copies.
Deliberately storing copies of data to make reads faster, at the cost of keeping the copies in sync.
An extra data structure that lets a database find rows without scanning the whole table, at the cost of storage and slower writes.
A balanced tree of sorted keys with many children per node, so any key is a few disk reads away. The default index in most relational databases.
Log-structured merge tree: buffers writes in memory, flushes them as sorted files and merges files in the background. Fast writes, more work for reads.
An index on several columns in a fixed order. It helps queries that filter on a leading prefix of those columns.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index alone.
When one logical write causes several physical writes, for example updating indexes or rewriting files during compaction.
Reading every row of a table to answer a query, which is what happens without a useful index.
The time between sending a request and receiving its response.
How much work a system completes per unit of time, such as requests per second.
How much data a link can carry per second.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall. p99 latency of 200 ms means 99% of requests finish within 200 ms.
The latency of the slowest requests, such as p99 or p99.9. At scale, most users hit the tail somewhere.
The total time a request may take, split across the steps it passes through.
Sending a second copy of a slow request to another replica and using whichever answers first, to cut tail latency.
Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine. Simple, but limited and with a single point of failure.
Handling more load by adding more machines and spreading work across them.
A service that keeps no per-user data between requests, so any instance can handle any request.
A component that spreads incoming requests across several servers and stops sending to unhealthy ones.
Balancing by connection (IP and port) without looking inside requests. Fast, but unaware of URLs or headers.
Balancing by request content such as path, header or cookie, which enables smarter routing at more cost.
Sending each new request to the next server in turn.
Sending each new request to the server with the fewest requests in progress.
A periodic probe that tells a load balancer whether an instance is able to serve traffic.
Picking two servers at random and sending the request to the less busy one. Spreads load almost as well as checking every server.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down.
Keeping a copy of frequently used data in faster storage so later reads skip the slow source.
The share of requests a cache answers itself. A hit rate of 90% means only 10% of requests reach the source.
The application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and stores the result in the cache.
A cache that loads missing data from the source itself, so the application only ever talks to the cache.
Every write goes to the cache and the source at the same time, keeping them in sync at the cost of slower writes.
Writes go to the cache first and reach the source later, which is fast but risks losing data if the cache fails.
Time to live: how long a cached value or DNS answer may be used before it must be refreshed.
Least recently used: when the cache is full, drop the item that has gone unused the longest.
Least frequently used: when the cache is full, drop the item that has been used the fewest times.
Removing or updating cached copies when the source data changes.
Many requests miss the cache at the same moment (often when a hot key expires) and all hit the database together.
Content delivery network: servers around the world that cache content close to users.
Keeping copies of the same data on several machines for availability, durability or read capacity.
One node (the leader or primary) accepts writes and streams them to followers (replicas) that serve reads.
Several nodes accept writes and exchange them, which needs a plan for conflicting writes.
Clients write to and read from several replicas directly and use quorums to decide what is current.
The delay before a write on the leader appears on a follower.
A guarantee that after you write something, your own later reads see it.
Promoting a replica to take over when the leader fails.
The minimum number of replicas that must take part in a read or write. With R + W > N, every read overlaps the latest write.
Splitting data across machines so each one holds only part of it.
Assigning keys to shards by key range, like A–F and G–M. Good for range scans, prone to hot spots.
Assigning keys to shards by a hash of the key, which spreads load evenly but loses ordering.
A shard or key that receives far more traffic than the rest.
Moving data between shards when you add or remove machines.
Placing keys and nodes on a ring so that adding or removing a node moves only the keys next to it.
Giving each physical node many points on a consistent-hashing ring so load spreads more evenly.
A buffer between producers and consumers. Each message is processed by one consumer.
Each published message is delivered to every subscriber of its topic.
A consumer’s signal that it has finished a message, so the queue can stop redelivering it.
Every message is delivered, but some may arrive more than once, so consumers must handle duplicates.
Messages are never duplicated, but some may be lost.
The effect of each message happens once. In practice this comes from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
Where messages go after failing too many times, so they stop blocking the queue and can be inspected.
Slowing down or rejecting producers when consumers cannot keep up, instead of letting work pile up without limit.
Every read sees the most recent completed write.
If writes stop, all replicas eventually return the same value; until then reads may be stale.
Operations that depend on each other are seen in the same order by everyone; unrelated ones may be seen in any order.
The system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data and every operation took effect at one instant.
A failure that splits machines into groups that cannot talk to each other.
During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency (refuse some requests) and availability (answer, possibly with stale data).
Extends CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.
Getting several machines to agree on one value or order of events, even when some fail.
A consensus algorithm with an elected leader that replicates a log of commands to followers.
Capping how many requests a client may make in a period of time.
A rate limiter where tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one; bursts are allowed up to the bucket size.
A rate limiter that queues requests and lets them out at a steady rate, smoothing bursts.
Counting requests per fixed interval, such as per minute. Simple, but allows double bursts at window edges.
Counting requests over the last N seconds at any moment, which avoids the edge bursts of fixed windows.
An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
A unique id sent with a request so the server can recognise a retry and return the first result instead of acting twice.
Retrying a failed request after waiting longer each time, so a struggling service gets room to recover.
Random variation added to retry delays so many clients do not retry at the same instant.
Quick, rounded arithmetic to size a system before designing it: requests per second, storage, bandwidth.
Queries (or requests) per second.
The number of distinct users who use a product on a given day.
How much busier the busiest period is than the average, often 2–5× for consumer products.
Average number of items in a system = arrival rate × average time each spends inside (L = λW).
What a system must do: the features and user actions it supports, such as posting a photo or reading a feed.
How well a system must do its job: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability and cost targets.
The share of time a system answers requests successfully, often written in nines: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month.
A target for a measurable behavior of a service, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding or p99 latency under 300 ms, used to decide when reliability work comes first.
Copying a new post into every follower's precomputed feed when it is published. Reads become fast, but posts from accounts with millions of followers are expensive.
Building a feed when it is requested by pulling recent posts from everyone the reader follows. Writes stay cheap; each read does more work.
A list of numbers (a vector) that represents an item such as a word, image, user or product, placed so that similar items end up close together.
A retrieval model with one network for users or queries and one for items. Each produces an embedding, and a high similarity between the two predicts a match.
Finding vectors close to a query vector without comparing it with every one, trading a little accuracy for large speedups, using indexes such as HNSW or IVF.
A store that indexes embeddings for fast similarity search, usually with filtering on metadata.
The first, cheap stage of a recommender or search system, which narrows millions of items to a few hundred for a heavier ranking model to score.
The second, more expensive stage of a recommender or search system, which scores a small set of candidates with rich features to decide the final order.
A system that computes, stores and serves model features, so the values used in training match the ones used when serving.
A gap between the data or feature logic a model was trained with and what it receives in production, which quietly lowers quality.
A change over time in the inputs a model receives compared with its training data, which can make its predictions worse.
Measuring a model on held-out historical data, with metrics such as precision, recall or AUC, before it reaches users.
An experiment that shows a change to a random share of users and compares their outcomes with a control group to measure its real effect.
The difficulty of making good predictions for new users or items that have little or no interaction history yet.
Answering with a language model after retrieving relevant passages and adding them to the prompt, so answers are grounded in your own data.
Splitting documents into passages small enough to embed and fit in a prompt, usually a few hundred tokens with some overlap.
Re-scoring the top retrieved results with a slower, more accurate model, such as a cross-encoder, before using them.
A fluent statement from a language model that is false or not supported by its sources.
The unit a language model reads and writes: a word or part of a word. In English, a token is about three quarters of a word on average.
The maximum number of tokens a language model can handle in one request, counting both the prompt and the answer.
Writing a number with 62 symbols (0–9, a–z and A–Z), so short strings cover huge ranges: 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion values.
Producing unique identifiers on many servers without one bottleneck, for example by handing out counter ranges or combining a timestamp, a machine id and a sequence number.
Combining keyword search, which is good at exact terms, with vector search, which is good at meaning, and merging the two result lists.

The attention keys and values a language model has already computed for earlier tokens, kept in GPU memory so each new token doesn't reprocess the whole sequence. It often limits how many requests fit on a GPU.
Adding new requests to a running batch and removing finished ones at every generation step, instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish, which keeps GPUs busy.
The two phases of language model generation: prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is compute-bound; decode produces output tokens one at a time and is limited by memory bandwidth.
How long a user waits before the first word of a streamed answer appears; mostly queueing plus prefill.
Splitting each layer's weight matrices across several GPUs so a model too large for one GPU can run, at the cost of fast GPU-to-GPU communication on every layer.
Storing model weights, and sometimes activations, in fewer bits (such as 8 or 4 instead of 16) to cut memory use and speed up inference at a small cost in accuracy.
A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. Accepted tokens come almost for free, speeding up generation without changing the output distribution.
A list of counters, one per replica, attached to each version of a value. Comparing two vector clocks shows whether one write happened before the other or whether they conflict.
Each node periodically shares what it knows, such as which nodes are alive, with a few random peers. Information spreads through the whole cluster in a few rounds without a central coordinator.
When a replica is unreachable, another node accepts its writes along with a hint naming the intended owner, and forwards them once the owner recovers.
A tree of hashes where each parent hashes its children. Two replicas compare roots and walk down only the branches that differ, finding mismatched keys quickly.
Splitting a video into short segments encoded at several qualities, so the player can switch quality every few seconds to match the viewer's bandwidth.
A compact bit array that answers "definitely not seen" or "probably seen" for an item. It uses little memory and never gives false negatives.
Reading a database's own change log to stream every insert, update and delete to other systems, such as a cache invalidator or a search index.
Rules a web crawler follows so it does not overload a site: obey robots.txt and wait between requests to the same host.
Waiting until input has paused for a short time, such as 100 ms, before acting on it, so a burst of keystrokes sends one request instead of many.
An address issued by Apple's or Google's push service that identifies one app install on one device. The server sends a push notification to this token, and it can change or expire.
A middle cache layer between CDN edge servers and the origin, so a cache miss at many edges becomes one request to the origin.
Showing whether a user is online, usually tracked with periodic heartbeats from their device and a short timeout.
When many requests for the same missing item arrive at once, only one fetches it from the source and the rest wait for and share its result.
A number that goes up by one for each new item in a stream, such as each message in a conversation, so receivers can order items and notice gaps.
A fingerprint for a document where similar documents get fingerprints that differ in only a few bits, so near-duplicate pages can be found cheaply.
Computing results continuously over events as they arrive, such as counts over the last five minutes, instead of in periodic batch jobs.
Converting a video from its uploaded format into other codecs, resolutions and bitrates so it can play well on every device and network.
A tree where each edge is one character, so all words that share a prefix share a path from the root. Finding everything that starts with a prefix is a short walk down the tree.
The crawler's to-do list: the queues of discovered URLs waiting to be fetched, ordered by priority and grouped by host.
A group communication step in which every worker contributes a value, such as its gradients, and every worker receives the combined result, such as their average.
When a user starts talking while a voice assistant is still speaking. The assistant should stop quickly and listen, like a person would.
How well a model's predicted probabilities match what actually happens. A calibrated model that predicts 2% for a group of cases sees about 2% of them turn out positive.
Periodically saving a long-running job's full state, such as model weights and optimizer state, so it can resume from that point after a failure instead of starting over.
A range around a measured value, such as an accuracy score, that likely contains the true value. A difference smaller than the interval may just be noise.
Training copies of the same model on different slices of each batch at the same time, then averaging their gradients so every copy stays identical.
Continuing to train an already trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so it follows a format, style or domain better.
Starting all the workers of a distributed job at the same time, or none of them. A training job that needs 64 GPUs cannot make progress with 63.
A curated, versioned set of test inputs with reference answers or grading rubrics, used to score every model or prompt change the same way.

Checks that run before and after a language model call, such as filters for unsafe content, leaked personal data or off-topic requests, so the system can block, rewrite or escalate a request or an answer.
A design in which a person reviews or approves certain automated decisions, such as large refunds, before they take effect, and takes over the cases the system can't handle.
A prompt crafted to get a language model to produce content its safety training or policy should refuse, often through role-play, encoding tricks or many small steps.
Detecting the structure of a page, such as columns, headings, tables and form fields, and the order in which its text should be read.
Using a language model with a written rubric to grade another model's answers, which scales evaluation far beyond human review. Its grades should be checked regularly against human ratings.
A fine-tuning method that freezes the original model weights and trains small extra matrices added to some layers. The result, an adapter, is often less than 1% of the model's size.

The share of the hardware's peak arithmetic rate that goes into useful model computation. Large training runs typically reach 30% to 50%; the rest is lost to communication, memory stalls and idle time.
Turning an image of text, such as a scanned page or a photo of a receipt, into machine-readable characters, usually with the position of each word.
Finding personal data such as names, phone numbers, emails or card numbers in text and masking or removing it before it is stored, logged or sent onward.
Splitting a model's layers into stages on different GPUs or servers and passing small micro-batches through them like an assembly line, so all stages work at once.

Keeping the KV cache for the opening tokens of a prompt, such as a system prompt or earlier chat turns, so a later request that starts with the same text skips recomputing them. It cuts time to first token and cost.
An attack in which text the model reads, typed by a user or found in a document, web page or tool result, contains instructions that try to override the system's own instructions.
Deliberately attacking your own system, by hand or with automated tools, to find failures such as jailbreaks before real attackers or users do.
Running a new model on live traffic without acting on its outputs, so its predictions, latency and errors can be compared with the current model before launch.
Converting spoken audio into text. Streaming recognizers emit partial transcripts while the person is still talking.
Generating spoken audio from text. Streaming systems start sending audio for the first words before the rest of the sentence is ready.

Letting a language model ask the application to run a named function, such as looking up an order or running tests, by producing a structured request with arguments. The application runs it and returns the result to the model.
A model that takes images and text together as input and produces text, so it can read a page, chart or photo and answer questions about it.
A small, fast model that labels each short slice of audio as speech or not speech, used to detect when someone starts and stops talking.
When one outcome is far rarer than the other, such as 1 fraud case per 1,000 payments. Accuracy becomes misleading, and training often samples or weights examples to compensate.
A system in which a language model works in a loop: it decides on a next step, calls a tool, reads the result and repeats until the task is done or it hands the task to a person.
Precision is the share of items a model flags that really are positive; recall is the share of all real positives that it flags. Raising one usually lowers the other.
A sequence of records that only grows at the end and is never changed in place. Each record has a position, called an offset, and each reader remembers how far it has read.
Replacing a card number with a random token that is useless if stolen. Only the payment provider or a secured vault can turn the token back into the card.
The number of distinct values something can take. In monitoring, it is the number of unique label combinations a metric has, and so the number of separate time series it creates.
A set of consumers that share the work of reading a partitioned topic. Each partition is read by one member at a time, and the group stores an offset per partition that says how far it has processed.
Storing each piece of data under a hash of its contents. Identical data gets the same name, so it is stored only once, and anyone can check that a block matches its name.
Syncing a changed file by sending only the parts that changed. The file is split into blocks, and only blocks the server doesn't already have are uploaded.
A record of money movements in which every transaction is written as debit and credit entries that sum to zero. A bug or a missing entry shows up as a balance that doesn't add up.

Replacing detailed data with coarser summaries as it ages, such as one point per hour that keeps the min, max, sum and count of the 360 ten-second points it replaces. Long-range queries then read far fewer points.

Splitting data into fragments and adding a few extra parity fragments, so the original can be rebuilt from any large enough subset. It survives several lost disks for roughly 1.5× the storage, instead of 3× for three full copies.
An index that quickly finds the points near a location. It usually divides the map into cells, such as geohashes, quadtree squares or hexagons, and searches only the cells around the query point.
The replicas of a partition that are fully caught up with its leader. A write is committed once all of them have it, and only they can become leader without losing committed data.

A service that stores files and large blobs as whole objects addressed by a key, such as Amazon S3. It is cheap, very durable and almost unlimited in size, but objects are replaced rather than edited in place.

Letting writers work without locks, then accepting a write only if the data still has the version the writer started from. If someone else changed it first, the write is rejected and must be retried or merged.
Regularly comparing your own records with an independent source, such as a payment provider's settlement report, to find and fix every mismatch.
A database built for streams of timestamped measurements, such as a server's CPU use every 10 seconds. It appends points in time order, compresses them heavily and answers queries over time ranges.

Writing an outgoing event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the change it describes. A separate relay then publishes outbox rows, so an event is never lost or sent for a change that didn't commit.
